title: Tutorial: Quick & Easy Parser Combinators
content_html:
Parsing is a fundamental skill for any programmer. Understanding how text is read by the computer, and better yet knowing how to tell the computer to read text in a robust manner, opens the door to solving problems in completely new ways. There have been many times for me that knowing how to make a parser has had utility. A good example is GQLM, a macro pre-processor step for GraphQL, which addressed two annoyances I had with the language (and AWS AppSync). Another example is validating an email generator for AWS SES; since the parser code for the high level email grammar is pretty concise. And of course, making your own programming languages (which I would call a personal hobby) requires understanding parsing to some degree as well.

Recently, I've wanted to rewrite an old project of mine, a simple dice roller, in Gambit. I have a lot of more complex functionality I've been wanting to add and experiment with, particularly the ability to roll against hex-flower tables or use Markov chains to model NPC emotions and other stateful things. I also want to give the tool a proper "language" for rolling dice, which is where parsing comes in.

Unfortunately, Gambit doesn't have any nice (or at least, easy to find) libraries for writing parsers, so I need to make my own. And because this is my tenth time doing this at this point, I thought I would run through the basic structure both for my own future reference and so you-who-reads-this-blog can also quickly write your own parsing toolkit. The approach I'll use is called "parser combinators", which are particularly popular in Haskell (and other functional languages) but are generally good for building parsers quickly.

Parser combinators have the advantage of being extremely quick to work with and build, and produce very readable code. In the example implementation in this tutorial, you will see that our parser code ends up looking remarkably close to the grammar we're trying to parse. This comes with the downside of parser combinators being slow compared to well-made LL or LR parsers (which is why tools like Bison exist); though in practice I still prefer working with them for the readability benefits. Another hitch, which I'll explain when it comes up, is shared with other LL parsers: that being that left-recursive grammars can and will cause infinite loops. This part always trips me up when I need to write a parser again for whatever reason, but I'll explain how to work around it both in the grammar and parser code itself.

This blog will show an implementation in Scheme, however the principles here are the same in any language, however your language must support first-class functions and closures to use this approach. Thankfully, most modern languages do, and so you should be able to use this tutorial to implement your own parsing library in any of JavaScript, Python, Rust, or whatever your favourite language is.

What are Parser Combinators? Actually, what are Combinators?

Simply put, a combinator is just a function that takes some number of other functions and returns a function that combines or modifies their functionality in some way. Some examples:

  • g = identity(f) where calling g(1) is the same as calling f(1).
  • g = complement(f) where calling g(1) is the same as calling not f(1).
  • g = flip(f) where calling g(1, 2) is the same as calling f(2, 1).
  • g = compose(f, h) where calling g(1) is the same as calling f(h(1)).

And the list goes on.

Parser combinators work the same way. We have a one or a few basic functions that check if the first "unit" of the list we give them matches their parameter, and if it does we return true along with the matched value and remainder of the list. In the implementation shown here, I'm going to work with characters and strings, but this same approach works with lexer tokens, numbers, or whatever else you want to use.

Then, we have some functions that order those unit matchers into larger structures that are more useful to us. Let's go over a really simple pseudocode example:

  • char(x) produces a function (parser) that returns true if the first character of the given string is "x".
  • sequence(parser...) produces a parser that returns true if the string matches, in order, all parsers given to it.
  • So we can make a parser g = sequence(char("a"), char("b"), char("c")).
    • g("abc") returns true.
    • g("def") returns false.
    • g("abcdef") returns true as well as the remainder of the input string, "def".

If this seems simple, that's because it is. Parser combinators are simple to implement, simple to understand, and yet more powerful than tools such as regex. It's a wonder that more languages don't implement them as core functionality.

What Combinators Do We Need?

Before we get started actually writing the code, we first need to understand what it is we need to implement. The formal definition of regex gives us a good starting point. You likely already know regex, but the extended regex that you're used to from your language of choice is a bit more than we need here. The formal definition is far simpler, with 3 constants:

  • The empty set, ∅.
  • The set containing only the empty string, ε.
  • The set containing a single character.

And 3 operations:

  • Concatenation, such as ab to first match a and then b.
  • Alternation, such as a|b to match either a or b.
  • Kleene star, to such as a to match zero or more a's sequentially.

Aside from the empty set, which we don't really need, this is also all the specification we need for parsing. In other words, the base library only has 5 functions:

  • A parser that matches an empty input (such as "" or an empty list, or #EOF).
  • A parser that matches a single unit of whatever it is we're parsing. This can either be a single character, or it can be a lexer token, or a struct, or object, or whatever else.
  • A parser that parses a sequence (from left to right) of parsers (this is our sequence function from before).
  • A parser that parses either of the parsers given to it, either.
  • A parser that parses a given parser zero or more times, many.

We will then extend our library to create a bunch of shortcuts. For example, one-or-more could be implemented as a sequence of a single parser, followed by many of the same parser.

Constant Parsers

Our first parser, the empty input, is easy (I mean none of this is that complex), but it sets the structure for how we'll implement all of our parsers.

Each parser is a function which returns a function that takes a single input parameter. For our eof parser, the returned function checks if input is an empty string. If it is, we return two values: the first being the matched text (in this case an empty list, the Scheme equivalent of null), and the second being the remaining text in the string (which is an empty string, because we have nothing left over). If the input is not an empty string, we return False. 

(define (eof)
  (lambda (input)
    (if (= 0 (string-length input))
        (cons '() "")
        #f)))

Note for those not familiar with Scheme, cons is just creating a pair of two values here. The function car will access the first value, and cdr will access the second value.

Simple enough, right?

Next up is the unit parser. We're doing string parsing here, so our unit is a single character. We will do this by passing the character value into the function so we can reference it in the returned closure. If the string is not empty, and the first character is the character we specified, we return the matched character and then the remaining string. 

(define (char chr)
  (lambda (input)
    (if (and (< 0 (string-length input))
           (equal? (string-ref input 0) chr))
        (cons chr (substring input 1 (string-length input)))
        #f)))

And that's it for the constants. You can of course substitute char for a different parser, such as struct or token or any other unit.

Basic Combinators

Let's have a look at sequence first, which I'm going to shorten just to seq. The seq function takes a list of parsers as input. It then iterates through each parser, adding the result on to the previous result. If it ever fails to parse, then return false immediately.

Procedural programmers avert your eyes, I'm using recursion and not loops. 

(define (seq . parsers)
  (define (match-next p result rest)
    (if (= p (length parsers))
      (cons result rest)
      (let* ((parser (list-ref parsers p))
             (parse-result (parser rest)))
        (if parse-result
            (match-next (+ 1 p)
                        (append result (list (car parse-result)))
                        (cdr parse-result))
            #f))))
  (lambda (input)
    (match-next 0 '() input)))

We can test this function to prove that it works, including already functioning with nested sequence parsers. 

((seq (char #\f) (char #\o) (char #\o)) "foo") ((seq (char #\f) (char #\o) (char #\o)) "foodie") ((seq (char #\f) (seq (char #\o) (char #\o))) "foodie")

either is similarly simple. It takes a list of parsers as input, and iterates through them until one of them parses, then returns the successful result. If none of the parsers match, it returns false. 

(define (either . parsers)
  (define (test-parser p input)
    (if (null? p)
      #f
      (let* ((parser (car p))
             (parse-result (parser input)))
        (if parse-result
            parse-result
            (test-parser (cdr p) input)))))
  (lambda (input)
    (test-parser parsers input)))

And some simple tests (for brevity, I won't prove that it handles nesting and remainder - just take my word for it): 

((either (char #\a) (char #\b)) "a") ((either (char #\a) (char #\b)) "b")

And the last of our core functions, many. many takes a single parser and matches it against the input string until it fails. many never returns False, because technically zero matches is allowed. 

(define (many parser)
  (define (match-next result rest)
    (let ((parse-result (parser rest)))
      (if parse-result
        (match-next (append result (list (car parse-result)))
                    (cdr parse-result))
        (cons result rest))))
  (lambda (input)
    (match-next '() input)))

And tests (again, made more concise for brevity): 

((many (char #\a)) "a") ((many (char #\a)) "") ((many (char #\a)) "aaabbb")

And that's finished off our core functions. Even with just this, we can already implement any parser we want, but it'll be annoying and we can make the core library a bit more useful.

Improving the Core: Parsing Arithmetic

To do that, let's define a specific parsing problem: parsing basic arithmetic expressions. We want to handle the following:

  1. All the basic arithmetic operations, so addition, subtraction, multiplication and division; with the correct order of operations.
  2. Whole numbers, decimal numbers, and negative numbers.
  3. Brackets to change the order of operations.

We'll also ignore whitespace and strip it from the input to the parser. This is the grammar we'll write: 

<expression> ::= <sum>
<sum> ::= <product> (("+" | "-") <product>)*
<product> ::= <value> (("*" | "/") <value>)*
<value> ::= <number> | <closed expression> | <negation>
<negation> ::= "-" <value>
<closed expression> ::= "(" <expression> ")"
<number> ::= <digit> <digit>* "." <digit>* | <digit> <digit>*
<digit> ::= "0" | "1" | "2" | ... | "8" | "9"

If you're not sure how to read BNF, Wikipedia has a great explanation.

One thing to note is the way we've defined our <sum> and <product> grammars is not left-recursive. This is because, like any LL parser, parser combinators will loop infinitely on a left-recursive grammar, such as the one below: 

<sum> ::= <sum> ("+" | "-") <sum> | <value>

We can expand this grammar out in our heads, but the computer will struggle with it, because it will infinitely try to parse that first <sum>.

Let's define digit first. We can do this by cheating a bit with Scheme's apply function. Basically, we just use map to build a list of char parsers from a list of characters (each digit), then pass that to either. 

(define digit
  (apply either
       (map
        (lambda (x) (char x))
        (string->list "0123456789"))))

(digit "1") will return (#\1 . "").

With digit, we can define number as essentially identical to our grammar above: 

(define number
  (either
   (seq digit
      (many digit)
      (char #\.)
      (many digit))
   (seq digit
      (many digit))))

There are a few improvements to be made here though. Specifically, with some BNF extensions we could shorten this grammar by making the decimal optional, and making digit "one or many" and not just many. 

number ::= <digit>+ ("." <digit>*)?

We can, of course, add these two as combinators just as well.

One or many is the easiest, it's really just a sequence of one parser followed by many of the same parser: 

(define (one-plus parser)
  (seq parser (many parser)))

One thing to note is that this won't return one flat list because of how the seq combinator works. Instead, we will see something like this: 

((one-plus (char #\a)) "aaa")

We can fix this behaviour with post-processing, which we'll go over soon.

Before that, let's implement our optional parser opt. opt checks a particular parser against its input. If it succeeds, then easy we just return the output of the parser. Otherwise, we want to return null and the input string; we don't return False here, because the parser did succeed. 

(define (opt parser)
  (lambda (input)
    (let ((res (parser input)))
      (if res
        res
        (cons '() input)))))

With these two additional combinators, we can now implement the shorter version of the grammar! 

(define number
  (seq (one-plus digit)
       (opt (seq (char #\.)
               (many digit)))))

In my opinion this is perhaps less readable, but it is nicer to make this a bit more concise.

There's just one problem: our output when parsing a number is kind of horrible: 

(number "123.4")

Wouldn't it be great if this just returned us an actual number? Well, that's where post-processing comes in.

Post-Processing

Sometimes, as the output of one of our parsers, we want to do more than return just the raw list of units. This is most obvious in our number example, I would love to have that output either the string "123.4" or just the number itself 123.4. This can be done with post-processing, which is another combinator that simply runs a parser, and if it succeeds in parsing it runs a given function against the returned parse tree. Let's call this function post-process. 

(define (post-process processor parser)
  (lambda (input)
    (let ((res (parser input)))
      (if res
        (cons (processor (car res))
              (cdr res))
        #f))))

Now we can adjust our number parser like so: 

(define number
  (post-process
   (lambda (result)
     (string->number
      (list->string
       (flatten result))))
   (seq (one-plus digit)
      (opt (seq (char #\.)
                (many digit))))))

And now our parser outputs numbers properly: 

(number "123.4")

Implementing the Rest

We now have enough to implement every single grammar rule, so here's the rest of them. 

(define digit
  (apply either
       (map
        (lambda (x) (char x))
        (string->list "0123456789"))))

(define number
  (post-process
   (lambda (result)
     (string->number
      (list->string
       (flatten result))))
   (seq (one-plus digit)
      (opt (seq (char #\.)
                (many digit))))))

(define (closed-expr input)
  ((post-process
    (lambda (res)
      (list (cadr res)))
    (seq
     (char #\()
     expression
     (char #\)))) input))

(define (negation input)
  ((post-process
    (lambda (res)
      (- (cadr res)))
    (seq (char #\-)
       value)) input))

(define value
  (either number closed-expr negation))

(define product
  (seq
   value
   (many (seq (either (char #\*)
                    (char #\/))
            value))))

(define sum
  (seq
   product
   (many (seq (either (char #\+)
                    (char #\-))
            product))))

(define expression sum)

You can see that we can more or less follow the exact BNF grammar for our rules. One thing to note is that we've made closed-expr and negation functions rather than variables here. This is so when they are called, they will see the declaration of expression and value, which depend on these two. This is called lazy loading.

This grammar does parse: 

(expression "2*(3+-4)*5")

However, this can still be improved.

Cleaning Up

The first thing that comes to mind is all those empty lists hovering about. Those are the result of our use of many in the sum and product parsers, as the many can of course match nothing, in which case we get an empty list.

To fix this, we can simply add the following as a post-processor for sum and product: 

(define (strip-null-cdr res)
  (if (equal? '() (last res))
      (car res)
      res))

Now we get a much more sane result. 

(expression "2*(3+-4)*5")

If you're working in a non-Scheme language, this is likely where you can get off. You may want to add a post-processor that converts this into a parser node, instead of just using a list, but essentially the next step after this is making an interpreter, which I won't be covering here.

Interpreting the Result

However, if you're using Scheme or Lisp, there is one last trick that we can do here as a shortcut to build a full interpreter: we can reorder this tree into a valid Lisp form, then pass it to eval.

This is actually fairly easy to do, all you need is one more post-processor for our two left-associative operations sum and product to reorganise the whole tree and convert the operation characters into symbols.

Our output at the moment is not really a true parse tree in the working sense. It lacks associativity, and is essentially just a list of values. What we want to do is re-orgnise it into a left-assocative tree, and we can do this with a fairly simple algorithm:

  1. Start with the left-most node of the list.
  2. Iterate over each node in the remaining list.
  3. In each iteration, make a list with 3 elements; the operator of the current iteration's operation, the value from the previous iteration (the left-most node to start), and the remainder of the operation.
  4. Save the value of that iteration and use it in the next iteration.
  5. Keep going until you hit the end of the list.

In Scheme, this gives us the following code: 

(define (left-associative res)
  (define (iter acc next)
    (if (null? next)
      acc
      (let ((op (car next)))
        (iter (list (string->symbol (list->string (list (car op))))
                    acc
                    (cadr op))
              (cdr next)))))
  (if (and (pair? res) (not (symbol? (car res))))
      (iter (car res) (cadr res))
      res))

You will notice we only adjust the list here if the first item in the list is not a symbol. If we don't do this, the post-processor in sum will try to reorganise the already left-associative output of product. If our expression only has product operations, then this will cause an error, so that catch prevents doubling up. It's a bit messy, but then again the better option here is to parse this into an actual tree. This is just a hack possible in Lisp.

Which we can then add as a post-processor to sum and product, and run the parser to observe the output: 

(expression "1+2+3") (expression "1*2*3") (expression "1+2*3") (expression "2*3+4") (expression "2+(3+-4)*5")

Wow! That looks a lot like Scheme, and we're maintaining the order of operations too! In fact, we can pass the first element of any output here directly to eval and it will work just fine: 

(eval (car (expression "1+2+3"))) (eval (car (expression "1*2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "1+2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "2*3+4"))) (eval (car (expression "2+(3+-4)*5")))

Oh wait, have we screwed something up here?

Take a look at the parser output again: (3+-4) is put into double brackets ((+ 3 -4)), which means that the result of that addition is being called as a function, (-1). That ain't right.

Fortunately, it's easy to see where the problem is: in the closed-expr. This parser is currently returning whatever it parses inside a list. This is a trivial fix, we'll just remove the list from the closed-expr post-processor, and just return the cadr of it's result.

And finally: 

(eval (car (expression "1+2+3"))) (eval (car (expression "1*2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "1+2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "2*3+4"))) (eval (car (expression "2+(3+-4)*5")))

Everything is as it should be!

Closing Up

Hopefully this has helped you learn a little bit more about parsing and the problems that good parsing can solve.

As I said at the start, the main reason I wrote this post is to accompany my own parser library implementation in Gambit. You can find that implementation here: I've called it Parque. The library is built using only base R7RS, so it should work in any Scheme that supports R7RS' define-library.

While the implementation described in this blog post is already useful, it's more of a quick method for implementing combinators. I want Parque to be better than this, so I will extend it with some other combinators and a proper parser output record instead of just pairs. This blog post will remain as a reference for quickly implementing these functions.

It takes a list of parsers as input, and iterates through them until one of them parses, then returns the successful result. If none of the parsers match, it returns false. (define (either . parsers) (define (test-parser p input) (if (null? p) #f (let* ((parser (car p)) (parse-result (parser input))) (if parse-result parse-result (test-parser (cdr p) input))))) (lambda (input) (test-parser parsers input))) And some simple tests (for brevity, I won't prove that it handles nesting and remainder - just take my word for it): ((either (char #\a) (char #\b)) "a") ((either (char #\a) (char #\b)) "b") And the last of our core functions, many. many takes a single parser and matches it against the input string until it fails. many never returns False, because technically zero matches is allowed. (define (many parser) (define (match-next result rest) (let ((parse-result (parser rest))) (if parse-result (match-next (append result (list (car parse-result))) (cdr parse-result)) (cons result rest)))) (lambda (input) (match-next '() input))) And tests (again, made more concise for brevity): ((many (char #\a)) "a") ((many (char #\a)) "") ((many (char #\a)) "aaabbb") And that's finished off our core functions. Even with just this, we can already implement any parser we want, but it'll be annoying and we can make the core library a bit more useful. Improving the Core: Parsing Arithmetic To do that, let's define a specific parsing problem: parsing basic arithmetic expressions. We want to handle the following: All the basic arithmetic operations, so addition, subtraction, multiplication and division; with the correct order of operations. Whole numbers, decimal numbers, and negative numbers. Brackets to change the order of operations. We'll also ignore whitespace and strip it from the input to the parser. This is the grammar we'll write: <expression> ::= <sum> <sum> ::= <product> (("+" | "-") <product>)* <product> ::= <value> (("*" | "/") <value>)* <value> ::= <number> | <closed expression> | <negation> <negation> ::= "-" <value> <closed expression> ::= "(" <expression> ")" <number> ::= <digit> <digit>* "." <digit>* | <digit> <digit>* <digit> ::= "0" | "1" | "2" | ... | "8" | "9" If you're not sure how to read BNF, Wikipedia has a great explanation. One thing to note is the way we've defined our <sum> and <product> grammars is not left-recursive. This is because, like any LL parser, parser combinators will loop infinitely on a left-recursive grammar, such as the one below: <sum> ::= <sum> ("+" | "-") <sum> | <value> We can expand this grammar out in our heads, but the computer will struggle with it, because it will infinitely try to parse that first <sum>. Let's define digit first. We can do this by cheating a bit with Scheme's apply function. Basically, we just use map to build a list of char parsers from a list of characters (each digit), then pass that to either. (define digit (apply either (map (lambda (x) (char x)) (string->list "0123456789")))) (digit "1") will return (#\1 . ""). With digit, we can define number as essentially identical to our grammar above: (define number (either (seq digit (many digit) (char #\.) (many digit)) (seq digit (many digit)))) There are a few improvements to be made here though. Specifically, with some BNF extensions we could shorten this grammar by making the decimal optional, and making digit "one or many" and not just many. number ::= <digit>+ ("." <digit>*)? We can, of course, add these two as combinators just as well. One or many is the easiest, it's really just a sequence of one parser followed by many of the same parser: (define (one-plus parser) (seq parser (many parser))) One thing to note is that this won't return one flat list because of how the seq combinator works. Instead, we will see something like this: ((one-plus (char #\a)) "aaa") We can fix this behaviour with post-processing, which we'll go over soon. Before that, let's implement our optional parser opt. opt checks a particular parser against its input. If it succeeds, then easy we just return the output of the parser. Otherwise, we want to return null and the input string; we don't return False here, because the parser did succeed. (define (opt parser) (lambda (input) (let ((res (parser input))) (if res res (cons '() input))))) With these two additional combinators, we can now implement the shorter version of the grammar! (define number (seq (one-plus digit) (opt (seq (char #\.) (many digit))))) In my opinion this is perhaps less readable, but it is nicer to make this a bit more concise. There's just one problem: our output when parsing a number is kind of horrible: (number "123.4") Wouldn't it be great if this just returned us an actual number? Well, that's where post-processing comes in. Post-Processing Sometimes, as the output of one of our parsers, we want to do more than return just the raw list of units. This is most obvious in our number example, I would love to have that output either the string "123.4" or just the number itself 123.4. This can be done with post-processing, which is another combinator that simply runs a parser, and if it succeeds in parsing it runs a given function against the returned parse tree. Let's call this function post-process. (define (post-process processor parser) (lambda (input) (let ((res (parser input))) (if res (cons (processor (car res)) (cdr res)) #f)))) Now we can adjust our number parser like so: (define number (post-process (lambda (result) (string->number (list->string (flatten result)))) (seq (one-plus digit) (opt (seq (char #\.) (many digit)))))) And now our parser outputs numbers properly: (number "123.4") Implementing the Rest We now have enough to implement every single grammar rule, so here's the rest of them. (define digit (apply either (map (lambda (x) (char x)) (string->list "0123456789")))) (define number (post-process (lambda (result) (string->number (list->string (flatten result)))) (seq (one-plus digit) (opt (seq (char #\.) (many digit)))))) (define (closed-expr input) ((post-process (lambda (res) (list (cadr res))) (seq (char #\() expression (char #\)))) input)) (define (negation input) ((post-process (lambda (res) (- (cadr res))) (seq (char #\-) value)) input)) (define value (either number closed-expr negation)) (define product (seq value (many (seq (either (char #\*) (char #\/)) value)))) (define sum (seq product (many (seq (either (char #\+) (char #\-)) product)))) (define expression sum) You can see that we can more or less follow the exact BNF grammar for our rules. One thing to note is that we've made closed-expr and negation functions rather than variables here. This is so when they are called, they will see the declaration of expression and value, which depend on these two. This is called lazy loading. This grammar does parse: (expression "2*(3+-4)*5") However, this can still be improved. Cleaning Up The first thing that comes to mind is all those empty lists hovering about. Those are the result of our use of many in the sum and product parsers, as the many can of course match nothing, in which case we get an empty list. To fix this, we can simply add the following as a post-processor for sum and product: (define (strip-null-cdr res) (if (equal? '() (last res)) (car res) res)) Now we get a much more sane result. (expression "2*(3+-4)*5") If you're working in a non-Scheme language, this is likely where you can get off. You may want to add a post-processor that converts this into a parser node, instead of just using a list, but essentially the next step after this is making an interpreter, which I won't be covering here. Interpreting the Result However, if you're using Scheme or Lisp, there is one last trick that we can do here as a shortcut to build a full interpreter: we can reorder this tree into a valid Lisp form, then pass it to eval. This is actually fairly easy to do, all you need is one more post-processor for our two left-associative operations sum and product to reorganise the whole tree and convert the operation characters into symbols. Our output at the moment is not really a true parse tree in the working sense. It lacks associativity, and is essentially just a list of values. What we want to do is re-orgnise it into a left-assocative tree, and we can do this with a fairly simple algorithm: Start with the left-most node of the list. Iterate over each node in the remaining list. In each iteration, make a list with 3 elements; the operator of the current iteration's operation, the value from the previous iteration (the left-most node to start), and the remainder of the operation. Save the value of that iteration and use it in the next iteration. Keep going until you hit the end of the list. In Scheme, this gives us the following code: (define (left-associative res) (define (iter acc next) (if (null? next) acc (let ((op (car next))) (iter (list (string->symbol (list->string (list (car op)))) acc (cadr op)) (cdr next))))) (if (and (pair? res) (not (symbol? (car res)))) (iter (car res) (cadr res)) res)) You will notice we only adjust the list here if the first item in the list is not a symbol. If we don't do this, the post-processor in sum will try to reorganise the already left-associative output of product. If our expression only has product operations, then this will cause an error, so that catch prevents doubling up. It's a bit messy, but then again the better option here is to parse this into an actual tree. This is just a hack possible in Lisp. Which we can then add as a post-processor to sum and product, and run the parser to observe the output: (expression "1+2+3") (expression "1*2*3") (expression "1+2*3") (expression "2*3+4") (expression "2+(3+-4)*5") Wow! That looks a lot like Scheme, and we're maintaining the order of operations too! In fact, we can pass the first element of any output here directly to eval and it will work just fine: (eval (car (expression "1+2+3"))) (eval (car (expression "1*2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "1+2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "2*3+4"))) (eval (car (expression "2+(3+-4)*5"))) Oh wait, have we screwed something up here? Take a look at the parser output again: (3+-4) is put into double brackets ((+ 3 -4)), which means that the result of that addition is being called as a function, (-1). That ain't right. Fortunately, it's easy to see where the problem is: in the closed-expr. This parser is currently returning whatever it parses inside a list. This is a trivial fix, we'll just remove the list from the closed-expr post-processor, and just return the cadr of it's result. And finally: (eval (car (expression "1+2+3"))) (eval (car (expression "1*2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "1+2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "2*3+4"))) (eval (car (expression "2+(3+-4)*5"))) Everything is as it should be! Closing Up Hopefully this has helped you learn a little bit more about parsing and the problems that good parsing can solve. As I said at the start, the main reason I wrote this post is to accompany my own parser library implementation in Gambit. You can find that implementation here: I've called it Parque. The library is built using only base R7RS, so it should work in any Scheme that supports R7RS' define-library. While the implementation described in this blog post is already useful, it's more of a quick method for implementing combinators. I want Parque to be better than this, so I will extend it with some other combinators and a proper parser output record instead of just pairs. This blog post will remain as a reference for quickly implementing these functions.

blocks.html_en: Parsing is a fundamental skill for any programmer. Understanding how text is read by the computer, and better yet knowing how to tell the computer to read text in a robust manner, opens the door to solving problems in completely new ways. There have been many times for me that knowing how to make a parser has had utility. A good example is GQLM, a macro pre-processor step for GraphQL, which addressed two annoyances I had with the language (and AWS AppSync). Another example is validating an email generator for AWS SES; since the parser code for the high level email grammar is pretty concise. And of course, making your own programming languages (which I would call a personal hobby) requires understanding parsing to some degree as well.

blocks.html_en: Parser combinators have the advantage of being extremely quick to work with and build, and produce very readable code. In the example implementation in this tutorial, you will see that our parser code ends up looking remarkably close to the grammar we're trying to parse. This comes with the downside of parser combinators being slow compared to well-made LL or LR parsers (which is why tools like Bison exist); though in practice I still prefer working with them for the readability benefits. Another hitch, which I'll explain when it comes up, is shared with other LL parsers: that being that left-recursive grammars can and will cause infinite loops. content_html_zh:
解析是任何程序员的基本技能。 了解计算机如何读取文本，以及更好地了解如何告诉计算机以稳健的方式读取文本，为以全新方式解决问题打开了大门。 对我来说，很多时候知道如何制作解析器是有用的。 GQLM 就是一个很好的例子，它是 GraphQL 的宏预处理器步骤，它解决了我对该语言（和 AWS AppSync）的两个烦恼。 另一个例子是验证 AWS SES 的电子邮件生成器；因为高级电子邮件语法的解析器代码非常简洁。 当然，制作自己的编程语言（我称之为个人爱好）也需要在某种程度上理解解析。

最近，我想用 Gambit 重写我的一个旧项目，一个简单的骰子滚子。 我一直想添加和试验许多更复杂的功能，特别是滚动六角花表或使用马尔可夫链来模拟 NPC 情绪和其他有状态事物的能力。 我还想为该工具提供一种适当的“语言”来掷骰子，这就是解析的用武之地。

不幸的是，Gambit 没有任何好的（或者至少很容易找到）用于编写解析器的库，所以我需要创建自己的库。 因为这是我第十次这样做，所以我想我应该遍历一下基本结构，以供我自己将来参考，这样阅读此博客的人也可以快速编写自己的解析工具包。 我将使用的方法称为“解析器组合器”，它在 Haskell（和其他函数式语言）中特别流行，但通常适合快速构建解析器。

解析器组合器的优点是可以非常快速地使用和构建，并生成非常可读的代码。 在本教程的示例实现中，您将看到我们的解析器代码最终看起来非常接近我们尝试解析的语法。 与制作精良的 LL 或 LR 解析器相比，解析器组合器的缺点是速度慢（这就是 Bison 等工具存在的原因）；尽管在实践中我仍然更喜欢与它们一起工作以提高可读性。 另一个问题（我将在出现时解释）与其他 LL 解析器共享：左递归语法可以并且将会导致无限循环。 当我出于某种原因需要再次编写解析器时，这部分总是让我感到困惑，但我将解释如何在语法和解析器代码本身中解决它。

本博客将展示在Scheme中的实现，但是这里的原理在任何语言中都是相同的，但是您的语言必须支持一流的函数和闭包才能使用这种方法。 值得庆幸的是，大多数现代语言都可以，因此您应该能够使用本教程在 JavaScript、Python、Rust 或任何您喜欢的语言中实现您自己的解析库。

什么是解析器组合器？ 实际上，什么是组合器？

简而言之，组合器只是一个函数，它接受一些其他函数并返回一个以某种方式组合或修改它们的功能的函数。 一些例子：

  • g = Identity(f)，其中调用 g(1) 与调用 f(1) 相同。
  • g=complement(f)，其中调用 g(1) 与调用 not f(1) 相同。
  • g = Flip(f)，其中调用 g(1, 2) 与调用 f(2, 1) 相同。
  • g = compose(f, h)，其中调用 g(1) 与调用 f(h(1)) 相同。

这样的例子还在继续。

解析器组合器的工作方式相同。 我们有一个或几个基本函数来检查我们给它们的列表的第一个“单元”是否匹配它们的参数，如果匹配，我们返回 true 以及匹配的值和列表的其余部分。 在这里显示的实现中，我将使用字符和字符串，但同样的方法也适用于词法分析器标记、数字或您想要使用的任何其他内容。

然后，我们有一些函数将这些单元匹配器排序为对我们更有用的更大结构。 让我们看一个非常简单的伪代码示例：

  • char(x) 生成一个函数（解析器），如果给定字符串的第一个字符是“x”，则该函数返回 true。
  • 序列（解析器...） 生成一个解析器，如果字符串按顺序匹配给定的所有解析器，则该解析器返回 true。
  • 所以我们可以制作一个解析器 g =equence(char("a"), char("b"), char("c"))。 g("abc") 返回 true。 g("def") 返回 false。 g("abcdef") 返回 true 以及输入字符串“def”的其余部分。

如果这看起来很简单，那是因为事实确实如此。 解析器组合器易于实现、易于理解，而且比正则表达式等工具更强大。 令人惊奇的是，更多的语言没有将它们实现为核心功能。

我们需要什么组合器？

在我们开始实际编写代码之前，我们首先需要了解我们需要实现什么。 正则表达式的正式定义为我们提供了一个很好的起点。 您可能已经了解正则表达式，但是您在选择的语言中习惯使用的扩展正则表达式比我们在这里需要的要多一些。 正式的定义要简单得多，有 3 个常量：

  • 空集，∅。
  • 仅包含空字符串 ε 的集合。
  • 包含单个字符的集合。

和3个操作：

  • 连接，例如 ab 先匹配 a，然后匹配 b。
  • 交替，例如 a|b 匹配 a 或 b。
  • Kleene star，例如a，依次匹配零个或多个a。

除了我们并不真正需要的空集之外，这也是我们解析所需的所有规范。 也就是说，基础库只有5个函数：

  • 匹配空输入（例如“”或空列表或#EOF）的解析器。
  • 一个解析器，它匹配我们正在解析的任何内容的单个单元。 这可以是单个字符，也可以是词法分析器标记、结构体、对象或其他任何东西。
  • 一个解析器，用于解析解析器序列（从左到右）（这是我们之前的序列函数）。
  • 一个解析器，它解析给它的任何一个解析器。
  • 解析给定解析器零次或多次的解析器。

然后我们将扩展我们的库来创建一堆快捷方式。 例如，一个或多个可以被实现为单个解析器的序列，后面跟着许多相同的解析器。

常量解析器

我们的第一个解析器，空输入，很简单（我的意思是这些都没有那么复杂），但它为我们如何实现所有解析器设置了结构。

每个解析器都是一个函数，它返回一个采用单个输入参数的函数。 对于我们的 eof 解析器，返回的函数检查输入是否为空字符串。 如果是，我们返回两个值：第一个是匹配的文本（在本例中是一个空列表，Scheme 相当于 null），第二个是字符串中的剩余文本（这是一个空字符串，因为我们没有剩下任何内容）。 如果输入不是空字符串，我们返回 False。

(define (eof)
  (lambda (input)
    (if (= 0 (string-length input))
        (cons '() "")
        #f)))

对于那些不熟悉Scheme的人请注意，cons只是在这里创建一对两个值。 函数 car 将访问第一个值，而 cdr 将访问第二个值。

很简单，对吧？

接下来是单元解析器。 我们在这里进行字符串解析，因此我们的单位是单个字符。 我们将通过将字符值传递到函数中来完成此操作，以便我们可以在返回的闭包中引用它。 如果字符串不为空，并且第一个字符是我们指定的字符，则返回匹配的字符，然后返回剩余的字符串。

(define (char chr)
  (lambda (input)
    (if (and (< 0 (string-length input))
           (equal? (string-ref input 0) chr))
        (cons chr (substring input 1 (string-length input)))
        #f)))

这就是常数。 当然，您可以将 char 替换为不同的解析器，例如结构或令牌或任何其他单元。

基本组合器

让我们首先看一下序列，我将其缩短为 seq。 seq 函数将解析器列表作为输入。 然后它迭代每个解析器，将结果添加到前一个结果中。 如果解析失败，则立即返回 false。

程序程序员请移开视线，我使用的是递归而不是循环。

(define (seq . parsers)
  (define (match-next p result rest)
    (if (= p (length parsers))
      (cons result rest)
      (let* ((parser (list-ref parsers p))
             (parse-result (parser rest)))
        (if parse-result
            (match-next (+ 1 p)
                        (append result (list (car parse-result)))
                        (cdr parse-result))
            #f))))
  (lambda (input)
    (match-next 0 '() input)))

我们可以测试这个函数来证明它的工作原理，包括已经与嵌套序列解析器一起工作。

((seq (char #\f) (char #\o) (char #\o)) "foo") ((seq (char #\f) (char #\o) (char #\o)) "foodie") ((seq (char #\f) (seq (char #\o) (char #\o))) "foodie")

两者都同样简单。 它接受解析器列表作为输入，并迭代它们直到其中一个解析器解析，然后返回成功的结果。 如果没有一个解析器匹配，则返回 false。

(define (either . parsers)
  (define (test-parser p input)
    (if (null? p)
      #f
      (let* ((parser (car p))
             (parse-result (parser input)))
        (if parse-result
            parse-result
            (test-parser (cdr p) input)))))
  (lambda (input)
    (test-parser parsers input)))

还有一些简单的测试（为了简洁起见，我不会证明它可以处理嵌套和余数 - 请相信我的话）：

((either (char #\a) (char #\b)) "a") ((either (char #\a) (char #\b)) "b")

我们的最后一个核心功能有很多。 许多采用单个解析器并将其与输入字符串进行匹配，直到失败。 许多永远不会返回 False，因为技术上允许零匹配。

(define (many parser)
  (define (match-next result rest)
    (let ((parse-result (parser rest)))
      (if parse-result
        (match-next (append result (list (car parse-result)))
                    (cdr parse-result))
        (cons result rest))))
  (lambda (input)
    (match-next '() input)))

和测试（再次，为了简洁起见，更加简洁）：

((many (char #\a)) "a") ((many (char #\a)) "") ((many (char #\a)) "aaabbb")

我们的核心功能就这样完成了。 即使仅此，我们已经可以实现我们想要的任何解析器，但这会很烦人，我们可以使核心库​​更有用一点。

改进核心：解析算法

为此，我们定义一个特定的解析问题：解析基本算术表达式。 我们想要处理以下问题：

  1. 所有基本算术运算，例如加法、减法、乘法和除法；具有正确的操作顺序。
  2. 整数、小数和负数。
  3. 括号改变运算顺序。

我们还将忽略空格并将其从解析器的输入中删除。 这是我们要写的语法：

<expression> ::= <sum>
<sum> ::= <product> (("+" | "-") <product>)*
<product> ::= <value> (("*" | "/") <value>)*
<value> ::= <number> | <closed expression> | <negation>
<negation> ::= "-" <value>
<closed expression> ::= "(" <expression> ")"
<number> ::= <digit> <digit>* "." <digit>* | <digit> <digit>*
<digit> ::= "0" | "1" | "2" | ... | "8" | "9"

如果您不确定如何阅读 BNF，维基百科有很好的解释。

需要注意的一件事是我们定义 <sum> 和 <product> 语法的方式不是左递归的。 这是因为，像任何 LL 解析器一样，解析器组合器将在左递归语法上无限循环，如下所示：

<sum> ::= <sum> ("+" | "-") <sum> | <value>

我们可以在头脑中扩展这个语法，但是计算机会为此苦苦挣扎，因为它会无限地尝试解析第一个 <sum>。

我们首先定义数字。 我们可以通过使用Scheme 的apply 函数进行一些作弊来做到这一点。 基本上，我们只是使用 map 从字符列表（每个数字）构建字符解析器列表，然后将其传递给其中任何一个。

(define digit
  (apply either
       (map
        (lambda (x) (char x))
        (string->list "0123456789"))))

（数字“1”）将返回（#\1 . "").

使用数字，我们可以将数字定义为与上面的语法基本相同的：

(define number
  (either
   (seq digit
      (many digit)
      (char #\.)
      (many digit))
   (seq digit
      (many digit))))

不过，这里还需要进行一些改进。 具体来说，通过一些 BNF 扩展，我们可以通过使小数可选，并使数字“一个或多个”而不仅仅是多个来缩短此语法。

number ::= <digit>+ ("." <digit>*)?

当然，我们也可以将这两个添加为组合器。

一个或多个是最简单的，它实际上只是一个解析器的序列，后跟许多相同的解析器：

(define (one-plus parser)
  (seq parser (many parser)))

需要注意的一件事是，由于 seq 组合器的工作方式，这不会返回一个平面列表。 相反，我们会看到这样的东西：

((one-plus (char #\a)) "aaa")

我们可以通过后处理来修复此行为，我们很快就会讨论这一点。

在此之前，让我们实现可选的解析器选项。 opt 根据其输入检查特定解析器。 如果成功，那么我们只需返回解析器的输出即可。 否则，我们要返回 null 和输入字符串；我们在这里不返回 False，因为解析器确实成功了。

(define (opt parser)
  (lambda (input)
    (let ((res (parser input)))
      (if res
        res
        (cons '() input)))))

有了这两个额外的组合器，我们现在可以实现语法的较短版本！

(define number
  (seq (one-plus digit)
       (opt (seq (char #\.)
               (many digit)))))

在我看来，这可能可读性较差，但最好使其更简洁一些。

只有一个问题：解析数字时我们的输出有点可怕：

(number "123.4")

如果这只是返回给我们一个实际的数字不是很好吗？ 好吧，这就是后处理的用武之地。

后处理

有时，作为解析器之一的输出，我们想要做的不仅仅是返回原始单元列表。 这在我们的数字示例中最为明显，我希望输出字符串“123.4”或仅输出数字本身 123.4。 这可以通过后处理来完成，后处理是另一个简单运行解析器的组合器，如果解析成功，它就会针对返回的解析树运行给定的函数。 我们将此函数称为后处理。

(define (post-process processor parser)
  (lambda (input)
    (let ((res (parser input)))
      (if res
        (cons (processor (car res))
              (cdr res))
        #f))))

现在我们可以像这样调整我们的数字解析器：

(define number
  (post-process
   (lambda (result)
     (string->number
      (list->string
       (flatten result))))
   (seq (one-plus digit)
      (opt (seq (char #\.)
                (many digit))))))

现在我们的解析器正确输出数字：

(number "123.4")

实施其余部分

我们现在有足够的资源来实现每一条语法规则，所以这是其余的。

(define digit
  (apply either
       (map
        (lambda (x) (char x))
        (string->list "0123456789"))))

(define number
  (post-process
   (lambda (result)
     (string->number
      (list->string
       (flatten result))))
   (seq (one-plus digit)
      (opt (seq (char #\.)
                (many digit))))))

(define (closed-expr input)
  ((post-process
    (lambda (res)
      (list (cadr res)))
    (seq
     (char #\()
     expression
     (char #\)))) input))

(define (negation input)
  ((post-process
    (lambda (res)
      (- (cadr res)))
    (seq (char #\-)
       value)) input))

(define value
  (either number closed-expr negation))

(define product
  (seq
   value
   (many (seq (either (char #\*)
                    (char #\/))
            value))))

(define sum
  (seq
   product
   (many (seq (either (char #\+)
                    (char #\-))
            product))))

(define expression sum)

您可以看到，我们的规则或多或少可以遵循精确的 BNF 语法。 需要注意的一件事是，我们在这里创建了封闭表达式和否定函数而不是变量。 这样，当它们被调用时，它们将看到表达式和值的声明，这取决于这两者。 这称为延迟加载。

这个语法确实解析：

(expression "2*(3+-4)*5")

然而，这仍然可以改进。

清理

我首先想到的是那些盘旋的空列表。 这些是我们在和和乘积解析器中使用“许多”的结果，因为“许多”当然不能匹配任何内容，在这种情况下我们会得到一个空列表。

为了解决这个问题，我们可以简单地添加以下内容作为求和和乘积的后处理器：

(define (strip-null-cdr res)
  (if (equal? '() (last res))
      (car res)
      res))

现在我们得到了一个更加理智的结果。

(expression "2*(3+-4)*5")

如果您使用非Scheme 语言工作，这可能是您可以下手的地方。 您可能想要添加一个后处理器，将其转换为解析器节点，而不仅仅是使用列表，但本质上，下一步是创建一个解释器，我不会在这里介绍。

解释结果

然而，如果您使用的是Scheme或Lisp，我们可以在这里做最后一个技巧，作为构建完整解释器的捷径：我们可以将此树重新排序为有效的Lisp形式，然后将其传递给eval。

这实际上很容易做到，您所需要的只是为我们的两个左关联运算和和乘积多一个后处理器来重新组织整个树并将运算字符转换为符号。

我们目前的输出在工作意义上并不是真正的解析树。 它缺乏关联性，本质上只是一个值列表。 我们想要做的是将其重新组织成左关联树，我们可以使用相当简单的算法来做到这一点：

  1. 从列表最左边的节点开始。
  2. 迭代剩余列表中的每个节点。
  3. 在每次迭代中，创建一个包含 3 个元素的列表；当前迭代操作的运算符、上一次迭代的值（要开始的最左边的节点）以及操作的其余部分。
  4. 保存该迭代的值并在下一次迭代中使用它。
  5. 继续下去，直到到达列表的末尾。

在Scheme中，这给了我们以下代码：

(define (left-associative res)
  (define (iter acc next)
    (if (null? next)
      acc
      (let ((op (car next)))
        (iter (list (string->symbol (list->string (list (car op))))
                    acc
                    (cadr op))
              (cdr next)))))
  (if (and (pair? res) (not (symbol? (car res))))
      (iter (car res) (cadr res))
      res))

您会注意到，如果列表中的第一项不是符号，我们只会调整此处的列表。 如果我们不这样做，sum 后处理器将尝试重新组织已经左关联的乘积输出。 如果我们的表达式只有乘积运算，那么这将导致错误，因此 catch 可以防止加倍。 这有点混乱，但这里更好的选择是将其解析为实际的树。 这只是 Lisp 中可能的 hack。

然后我们可以将其作为后处理器添加到求和和乘积中，并运行解析器来观察输出：

(expression "1+2+3") (expression "1*2*3") (expression "1+2*3") (expression "2*3+4") (expression "2+(3+-4)*5")

哇！ 这看起来很像Scheme，而且我们也在维护操作顺序！ 事实上，我们可以将此处任何输出的第一个元素直接传递给 eval，它会正常工作：

(eval (car (expression "1+2+3"))) (eval (car (expression "1*2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "1+2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "2*3+4"))) (eval (car (expression "2+(3+-4)*5")))

哦等等，我们是不是搞砸了什么？

再次看一下解析器的输出：(3+-4) 被放入双括号 ((+ 3 -4)) 中，这意味着该加法的结果被作为函数调用 (-1)。 那是不对的。

幸运的是，很容易看出问题出在哪里：在 close-expr 中。 该解析器当前正在返回它在列表中解析的任何内容。 这是一个简单的修复，我们只需从 close-expr 后处理器中删除列表，然后返回其结果的 cadr 即可。

最后：

(eval (car (expression "1+2+3"))) (eval (car (expression "1*2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "1+2*3"))) (eval (car (expression "2*3+4"))) (eval (car (expression "2+(3+-4)*5")))

一切都是它应该的样子！
